title: Airbus Sends Specialists as Air India Pilot Faces Drug Test After Flight Drops 300 Feet
excerpt: The captain of a Phuket-Delhi flight that suddenly lost altitude returned an initial positive screening for psychoactive substances, prompting lab confirmation and a government probe.
body:
• An Air India A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi on August 4 suddenly lost approximately 300 feet of altitude during cruise, injuring 17 people including 4 crew members.
  • The captain returned a positive initial screening for psychoactive substances; samples have been sent for lab confirmation and both pilots are off roster.
  • Airbus confirmed Monday it is sending specialists to assist the investigation, which has been classified as a "serious incident" by India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau.
  • Flight Data Recorder and Cockpit Voice Recorder have been secured; India's DGCA has opened a formal probe.

What Happened on Flight AI2379

Air India flight AI2379, an Airbus A320 (registration VT-EXO), departed Phuket, Thailand, bound for Delhi on August 4 carrying 137 passengers and eight crew members. During cruise, the aircraft experienced what the airline described as a "sudden loss of altitude" — approximately 300 feet — before stabilizing and landing safely at Delhi at 11:07 a.m. local time.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=drZoS0MxNM0

The drop threw passengers from their seats. Thirteen passengers and four crew members were injured and taken to hospitals for medical evaluation, according to Air India. One cabin crew member reportedly suffered severe injuries.

"My father was sitting on the aisle seat and was having coffee. Suddenly, a big jolt happened, and he flew and hit the roof and fell on the floor."

— A passenger, speaking to The Times of India

Another passenger told news agency ANI: "The aircraft seemed to be moving normally but suddenly the turbulence began. I saw my sister thrown into the air from her seat. My mother was knocked on her head. We thought we would die."

Pilot's Drug Test Raises Questions

India's civil aviation ministry disclosed on Sunday that the captain returned an initial screening result for psychoactive substances under routine post-incident testing. Both flight crew members were screened as part of standard procedure.

Samples have been sent to a designated laboratory for confirmatory testing, the ministry said, without disclosing what substance was indicated. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation has taken both crew members off roster pending the outcome.

Air India said it was not informed of the screening results. "The results of the test have not been shared with Air India, and we are therefore not in a position to comment on any findings," a spokesperson said, adding that the airline conducts regular drug testing in compliance with civil aviation regulations.

Airbus Joins Investigation

European planemaker Airbus confirmed Monday it was sending specialists to assist the investigation, according to Reuters. The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has classified the incident as "serious" and secured the aircraft's Flight Data Recorder and Cockpit Voice Recorder for examination.

The 7-year-old A320 is now under scrutiny for potential hydraulic or autopilot system issues, though investigators have not yet released preliminary technical findings. The initial source reporting mentioned possible hydraulic failure and an autopilot disconnect, though official findings are pending.

Air India's Safety Record Under Scrutiny

The incident comes at a sensitive time for Air India, which is undergoing a major turnaround after Tata Group's acquisition from the Indian government. The airline recently tapped a former Ethiopian Airlines executive to lead its restructuring and announced plans to restore most international routes from September after summer-long disruptions.

Aviation experts note that altitude loss events during cruise, while rare, can result from multiple causes including turbulence, mechanical failure, or pilot error. Gary Leff, a travel industry analyst, told Fox News that injuries from turbulence occur in roughly one in 1.2 million departures.

What's Next

The AAIB investigation is expected to take weeks to months. The lab results from the captain's drug test will be a critical factor in determining whether the altitude loss was related to mechanical failure, environmental conditions, or crew performance. All injured passengers have been discharged, while crew members continue receiving medical care.
